title: Iran Rejects Shared Hormuz Plan, Demands Control Over Transit Lines; OPEC+ Signals Output Pause; US-Saudi Nuclear Deal Draws Proliferation Fire
subhead: Iran countered Oman's Gulf-backed proposal for joint Hormuz management with a plan routing traffic through Iranian waters, rejecting any return to free transit. Saudi Aramco shut its 400,000 bpd Jazan refinery after a Houthi strike. OPEC+ is set to pause output increases after September. And the US-Saudi nuclear agreement is drawing sharp criticism for lowering nonproliferation standards.

sections.heading: Iran Counters Oman's Hormuz Plan, Demands Exclusive Control Over Transit
sections.body:
Iran has formally rejected Oman's proposal for shared management of the Strait of Hormuz with voluntary shipping fees, instead offering a counterproposal that would route one direction of traffic entirely through Iranian waters and place part of the return lane under Iranian jurisdiction as well. Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi told state television on Tuesday that Iran 'no longer recognised' the International Maritime Organization's Traffic Separation Scheme, which has governed the waterway since 1968, and warned that the strait would remain closed if Muscat rejected Tehran's plan.

The Omani proposal — backed by Gulf states and modelled on the Strait of Malacca's voluntary contribution system — would have established joint regional management with no mandatory fees to Iran. A Gulf source and a Western diplomat told Reuters that Oman presented it to Tehran over the weekend. But Iran's counteroffer makes clear that Tehran's objective is formal administrative control, not just a toll. As a Forbes analysis noted, 'the fight over Hormuz is no longer only whether tankers can move. It is who writes the rules of movement, and whether those rules include a charge.'

The IMO's established shipping lanes remain unusable due to Iranian mines, with Tehran directing vessels through a northern route closer to its coast and the US offering assistance on a southern route near Oman. Gharibabadi also warned that Tehran would not allow any third country, even if invited by Oman, to de-mine the strait.
sections.whyItMatters: Iran is not bargaining over fees — it is seeking institutional control over a chokepoint carrying a fifth of global oil and LNG. The gulf between Oman's joint-management model and Iran's unilateral counterproposal suggests the strait will not return to free transit anytime soon, regardless of whether the US-Iran pause in strikes holds.

sections.heading: Saudi Aramco Shuts Jazan Refinery After Houthi Strike
sections.body:
Saudi Aramco has shut down its 400,000 barrel-per-day Jazan refinery following a Houthi missile and drone attack on Saturday, according to a note from consultancy IIR seen by Reuters. The strike damaged the facility's Integrated Gasification Combined Cycle complex and tank farm, with satellite imagery showing a tank fire. Repairs are tentatively expected to be completed by August 15.

The Houthis also claimed strikes on Aramco facilities in Yanbu — the Red Sea port that has served as Saudi Arabia's primary workaround for crude exports blocked by the Hormuz closure. The group declared a naval blockade against Saudi shipping on July 20, and on Tuesday claimed a ballistic missile attack on a Saudi oil tanker near Jizan. One tanker, the Encelia, sent a distress call after reporting a missile hit near Jizan, according to a maritime security source cited by Reuters.

The Jazan shutdown compounds an already strained fuel market. As Oilprice.com noted, refining margins had already surged to record highs, with gasoline, diesel, and jet fuel supplies tight and inventories thin before the strike. Unlike crude, which can be rerouted, stored, or discounted, finished fuel cannot bypass a refinery that is not running.
sections.whyItMatters: The war has followed Saudi Arabia's workaround. Yanbu was the exit point for crude circumventing Hormuz; now Houthi strikes threaten that route too. With 400,000 bpd of refining capacity offline and Red Sea transit under active threat, Saudi Arabia is losing options on both its eastern and western coasts simultaneously.

sections.heading: Oil Drops 5% on Diplomatic Pause Even as Hormuz Remains Closed
sections.body:
Brent crude fell $4.27 (4.8%) to settle at $84.09/barrel on Tuesday, hitting its lowest since July 13, while WTI dropped $3.35 (4.1%) to $79.26. The sell-off — extending a three-day, 16% decline — came on cautious hopes that the pause in US-Iran strikes could lead to a negotiated end to the conflict, despite the Strait of Hormuz remaining effectively closed.

President Trump said Monday there were 'good talks' underway with Iran, though Tehran has denied seeking negotiations. Bob Yawger, director of energy futures at Mizuho, noted that 'the market understands the situation is a mess and is trading lower because the two belligerent parties have not attacked each other in the past few days,' while pointing to the ongoing lack of Hormuz traffic and continued Houthi fire in the Red Sea.

Separately, Reuters reported that OPEC+ will likely pause oil output increases for three months from October, after completing the scheduled unwinding of voluntary cuts and facing potentially difficult talks over new production quotas. Sources said the pause reflects both the uncertainty around the US-Iran conflict and the group's effort to manage supply as demand forecasts shift.
sections.whyItMatters: Oil is pricing in de-escalation hope while the physical market tells a different story — Hormuz is closed, a major Saudi refinery is offline, and OPEC+ is about to stop adding supply. The gap between financial-market optimism and physical disruption is widening.

sections.heading: China Opens Direct Talks With Houthis for Red Sea Safe Passage
sections.body:
China has held direct talks with Yemen's Houthi movement to enable its tankers to sail through the southern Red Sea without being attacked, four sources told Reuters. The discussions come after at least two Chinese-owned oil tankers loaded with Saudi crude transited the Bab el-Mandeb Strait under apparent Houthi safe passage — the Hong Kong-flagged VLCC New Pearl departed the Red Sea on Monday carrying roughly 2 million barrels of Saudi crude to China.

Shipping patterns in the Red Sea are becoming more complex. Maritime analytics firm Windward reported that Bab el-Mandeb crossings fell roughly 22% in the six days after the Houthi blockade declaration on July 20. But on Monday, 28 vessels transited — a four-day high, though still well below July's peak of 46 on the 14th. Many tankers now openly broadcast Chinese or Russian crew nationalities to signal they are not affiliated with Western or Saudi interests.

Meanwhile, one VLCC — the Olympic Luck — exited the Red Sea via the Suez Canal on Sunday and began the longer voyage around Africa to Asia, becoming one of the first supertankers hauling Saudi crude to take the more expensive Cape route rather than risk Bab el-Mandeb.
sections.whyItMatters: China is building a parallel safe-passage system that insulates its energy imports from the conflict but deepens the selective nature of Red Sea disruption. Tankers flying non-Western flags get through; others reroute or halt. This is a de facto two-tier maritime regime — and it is being negotiated directly between Beijing and the Houthis, bypassing any US or naval coalition framework.

sections.heading: US-Saudi Nuclear Deal Draws Proliferation Criticism as South Korea Cries Double Standard
sections.body:
A CFR analysis published Monday warned that the US-Saudi nuclear cooperation agreement — announced July 22 — 'would set a dangerous new proliferation precedent' by departing from the 'gold standard' of nonproliferation conditions the US has required in past nuclear deals. Unlike the UAE's 2009 agreement, which voluntarily forswore enrichment, the Saudi deal appears to preserve the option for future enrichment and relies on bilateral rather than IAEA Additional Protocol safeguards.

President Trump further complicated the deal's prospects by linking it to Saudi normalization with Israel — a condition that could be a poison pill in Congress. The 123 agreement requires a 90-working-day congressional review, meaning the next Congress elected in November could weigh in.

South Korea, which has been seeking US consent for its own enrichment and reprocessing for years, has publicly noted the double standard. 'President Trump has put Saudi Arabia on the path to enriching uranium on its own soil, a demand South Korea has been making for decades,' the New York Times reported. US Energy Secretary Chris Wright has sought to clarify that the deal excludes enrichment technology exports, but the text's ambiguity on this point remains a core concern.
sections.whyItMatters: The deal's terms — enrichment ambiguity, bilateral safeguards, and an Israel-linked condition — represent a deliberate lowering of the nonproliferation bar for a strategic ally. If it proceeds, every nuclear-threshold state from Turkey to Egypt will cite it as precedent. The timing, amid a regional war and with IAEA access to Iran's bombed nuclear sites unresolved, makes the signal even sharper.

sections.heading: Saudi Aramco Explores Sidi Kerir Pricing as Red Sea Rerouting Costs Climb
sections.body:
Saudi Aramco is considering a new pricing mechanism for crude loading from Egypt's Sidi Kerir port for Asian buyers to reflect higher shipping costs after rerouting exports through the Suez-Mediterranean pipeline, according to Reuters and trading sources. Aramco has also offered additional crude cargoes for loading from Sidi Kerir as Houthi threats to Saudi shipping make southbound Red Sea transit riskier.

The shift reflects a structural adjustment: with Hormuz closed and Bab el-Mandeb under Houthi threat, the Suez-Mediterranean route has become a critical alternative for Saudi crude headed to Europe and — via the Cape — to Asia. But the longer voyage around Africa adds roughly $1-2 per barrel in freight costs, according to market estimates. Aramco is also weighing higher official selling prices for Asian buyers to offset these costs.
sections.whyItMatters: Aramco is building Red Sea disruption into its pricing architecture, not treating it as a temporary disruption. New pricing mechanisms for Sidi Kerir mean the market is adapting to a reality where Saudi crude reaches Asia via longer, more expensive routes — and those costs are being passed to buyers.

bottomLine: The day's developments reveal a widening gap between what markets are pricing and what the physical energy system is experiencing. Oil fell 5% on hopes of de-escalation, even as Iran formally demanded unilateral control over Hormuz transit, a 400,000 bpd Saudi refinery sat offline, and China negotiated its own safe-passage deal with the Houthis. The OPEC+ output pause from October will remove a potential supply cushion just as refining capacity tightens. Meanwhile, the US-Saudi nuclear deal is restructuring nonproliferation norms at the precise moment the IAEA cannot verify Iran's nuclear sites. The diplomatic optics suggest a pause; the operational reality suggests a system under compounding strain.
sources: Reuters, Al Monitor, Forbes, Oilprice.com, CFR, Bloomberg, NYT, AP, Al Jazeera, MSN, USA Today, Dawn, Oilprice.com, Gulf Times, India Today, Windward, IIR, Kpler, Times of Israel, CryptoBriefing
